entries.copy: The E105 five-point Likert form uses rating responses to form a full nine-type profile, top three candidates, a leading-candidate gap, and close-call comparison within one scoring context. It is a starting point for self-observation, and its scores are interpreted only within E105.

The FC144 two-option forced-choice form records relative preference signals across paired choices and can provide another observation after a close-call result. Both forms have the same evidence status. FC144 does not replace E105's primary candidate, top three candidates, or raw scoring facts, and its results are interpreted only within the FC144 scoring context.

E105 and FC144 use the same Enneagram interpretation framework but different response tasks, scoring sources, and error structures, so they do not share a scoring space. History, sharing, PDF, and retest surfaces retain each form's source. The page does not directly compare their values or interpret cross-form differences in the top three candidates as personality change.

Cross-form comparison is disabled. Unless a validated equivalence mapping becomes available, E105 and FC144 remain in separate scoring contexts, and history, sharing, and result-review surfaces do not infer improvement, decline, health status, or measurement precision from their differences.

This result supports personality-pattern reflection, self-observation, and dialogue. Current research does not support treating the Enneagram as a well-validated clinical scale. It is not used for mental-health judgment, treatment recommendations, hiring, job matching, competency evaluation, or individual risk assessment. Scores, leading candidates, close-call, diffuse, and response-quality states remain hypotheses to check against real situations.

A user-confirmed type records the user's own resonance after observation. It is not a system rescore or external confirmation. History and sharing surfaces present it only as a self-observation note; it does not overwrite the primary candidate, top three candidates, scorer output, or original scoring facts.

When triggered by low-quality signals, the results are still readable, but the interpretation boundaries are significantly narrowed. The page only retains light observation suggestions to avoid extending a single low-stability answer into a deterministic type of judgment; it gives priority to suggestions for retesting the same question type when the state is more stable and time is more sufficient. Switching forms can serve as another observation, but should not be used as a way to circumvent quality boundaries, find better answers, demonstrate personality changes, or compare score gains and losses.

Diffuse means the nine type signals do not yet form a clear leading pattern. The page lowers certainty about any one number and prioritizes the top three candidates, center distribution, recent counterexamples, and a seven-day observation task. Retesting provides another response sample; it does not automatically correct the result to a particular type.

A close-call means the first and second candidates are close. The page turns their differences into side-by-side comparison, counterexample checks, and seven-day observation questions without requiring a forced type decision.

entries.body: Start with the work cues, pace, and collaboration conditions that may draw your attention. Then compare environments that support this pattern with situations that make it costly. These are observation prompts, not conclusions about ability, performance, career fit, or employment decisions.
entries.module_purpose: Put the motivational differences between the primary type and Top3 into real-life task advancement methods, and make it clear that it only provides self-observation and communication clues, and cannot replace skill evidence, work experience, performance data, or organizational situation judgment.
entries.title: Work style summary

entries.body: Focus on the parts where you can contribute more stably to the team, such as closing, advancing, buffering, planning, connecting or structured judgment.
entries.module_purpose: Let users see the real value they bring to collaboration, rather than a general list of advantages.
entries.title: Collaboration advantage

entries.body: Point out the friction you might create in high-pressure or noisy collaborations, and write the costs not as moral criticism but as observable inertia.
entries.module_purpose: Help users see clearly "why others are stuck with me" and provide preventive explanations for relationships and work scenarios.
entries.title: Collaboration friction points

entries.body: Write only P0 Leadership tendencies that can be published online: Are you more likely to lead through standards, results, boundaries, buffers, or support rather than writing a complete management guide.
entries.module_purpose: Provide a shareable "How do you lead people" entry to the results page, leaving structural space for subsequent workplace expansion.
entries.title: leadership model

entries.body: Rather than writing an entire superior-subordinate pairing manual, describe what instructions, cadences, and feedback patterns may make it easier for you to stabilize.
entries.module_purpose: Turn personality reading into a more direct description of the experience of collaboration and being managed.
entries.title: A smoother way to be managed

entries.body: Use specific interaction scenarios to explain how you may express care in a relationship and how you may be misunderstood, and provide counterexamples to avoid inferring relationship needs based on type alone.
entries.module_purpose: Translate personality results into verifiable relationship communication cues: first look at the scenario, behavior and feedback, and then judge whether it fits; not a partner report, nor a conclusion about relationship needs.
entries.title: relationship needs

entries.body: Break the conflict into specific triggers, current misunderstandings, and a utterable repair language to help users review the interaction instead of drawing conclusions about the relationship.
entries.module_purpose: Provide verifiable conflict scripts: identify scenarios and triggers before attempting low-stakes fixes; don’t treat type as an explanation of who is right and who is wrong.
entries.title: conflict script

entries.body: Make communication suggestions into small cards that can be shared: first describe the situation that is easy to be misheard, and then give an expression that can be spoken.
entries.module_purpose: Provide low-certainty communication clues to help users and others calibrate facts, feelings, requests, and boundaries; do not treat types as relationship instructions or fixed rules for getting along.
entries.title: communication instructions

entries.average_expression: In most ordinary situations, people may fall back on familiar strategies for dealing with order, relationships, security, results, or tranquility.
entries.disclaimer: This is a spectrum of self-calibration and interpretation that only describes changes in expression in situations, not medical, mental health, or graded conclusions.
entries.recovery_action: First name the most obvious observable clue at the moment, and then choose a low-risk small action for verification; this is not a treatment suggestion, nor is it used to judge whether the state is good or bad.
entries.stable_expression: When genre inertia is not amplified by high-load situations, genre cues can be used to observe expressions that are more stable and have more leeway.
entries.strained_expression: When task load, interaction tension, or insufficient recovery space are superimposed, the same set of strategies may be used harder and narrower; this is just a review reminder.

technical_note.summary: Explains forms, score spaces, interpretation boundaries, data status, and privacy handling without making diagnostic, hiring, or deterministic personality claims.
technical_note.title: Technical Note

entries.body: The FermatMind Enneagram Test provides readable and observable hypotheses about personality patterns. It presents a primary candidate, top three candidates, the full nine-type profile, and close-call comparison before returning the reader to real situations. The technical note explains how modules are derived from response signals and interpretation rules, and which content remains theoretical or provisional.
entries.title: Test target

entries.body: The E105 five-point Likert form uses rating responses to form a full nine-type profile and top three candidates. The FC144 two-option forced-choice form records relative preference signals across paired choices. Both forms have the same evidence status but different response tasks and scoring sources; FC144 does not overwrite E105's primary candidate.
entries.title: E105 and FC144 two forms

entries.body: The score for E105 is derived from Likert intensity, and the score for FC144 is derived from relative preference of pairwise choice. They are both projected into the same result shell, but do not default into the same numerical comparison semantics. This is why same model is not equal to same score space.
entries.title: Score space boundary

entries.body: Dominance Gap describes the relative gap between Top1 and Top2 in the same form and the same score space, and is used to help the system choose a conservative tone of clear, close-call or diffuse. E105 is different from the question types and scoring units of FC144. The gap cannot be used as a unified ruler across forms, groups, or time; nor is it a measurement error range, statistical confidence interval, norm ranking, external validity proof, or personality certainty.
entries.title: Dominance Gap

entries.body: The current system will output clear, close_call, diffuse, low_quality and other explanation ranges. They control the tone of the results page, the visibility of modules, and recommended actions, rather than claiming that a certain number has been absolutely proven. clear means that the explanations of the same form this time are more concentrated; close_call means that they need to be read side by side; diffuse means that the tone of a single number needs to be reduced; low_quality means that the answer signal is not enough to support strong explanations.
entries.title: Confidence Band

entries.body: When Top1 and Top2 are close, the system will not pretend to be more certain than the data, but will enter the task of pair analysis and 7-day observation. close-call is a ambiguity management bit, not a judgment modification mechanism.
entries.title: Close-call

entries.body: Diffuse refers to the simultaneous emergence of multiple type clues in the profile shape, and Top1 and adjacent candidates are not enough to support a strong primary type narrative. It is a state of reduced certainty in the scope of interpretation, not failure, ineffectiveness, confusion, or low-quality responses. The system will shift the reading focus from a single number to the Top 3 common themes, three-center distribution, evidence contrary to recent life, and repeatable observation tasks; only if these clues continue to appear in real situations are they suitable to continue to narrow the interpretation.
entries.title: Diffuse

entries.body: When a true quality signal triggers, the system enters the low_quality boundary. The function of low_quality in P0 is to narrow the tone and recommend retesting the same form, rather than labeling users unreliable.
entries.title: Low-quality

entries.body: Test-retest stability is an indicator that will be tracked in subsequent Technical Notes. P0 first discloses the definition and collection plan, and does not commit to specific stability rate figures in advance. Stability evidence needs to distinguish between retests of the same form, cross-form agreement, short-term status fluctuations, and user feedback; when the sample, time interval, and answer quality are insufficient, the page will not interpret a retest difference as a personality change.
entries.title: Retake Stability

entries.body: The agreement between E105 and FC144 is used to evaluate the overlap between the two question types on Top1 or Top3, rather than proving that the scores can be directly compared between the two. P0 first defines indicators and collection directions, and then evaluates whether to disclose specific indicators based on samples. Agreement can only show the degree of agreement between the two question types in the ranking of candidates, and cannot independently prove the external validity, clinical validity or career prediction ability of the Enneagram model.
entries.title: E105 / FC144 Agreement

entries.body: The user's Day7 resonance feedback and user_confirmed_type will be entered into the history as self-observation evidence for research and content calibration, but will not silently overwrite the primary_candidate. User feedback is an observation layer, not a re-judgment by the system; it can prompt which narratives need to be downgraded, add counterexamples, or rewrite expressions, but it cannot directly equate resonance with measurement accuracy.
entries.title: Resonance Feedback

entries.body: This test is used for understanding personality patterns and self-observation, and is not used for clinical diagnosis, recruitment screening, treatment recommendations, hard judgments on health levels, or absolute personality characterization. Wing, arrow, subtype and development stage languages ​​are only reserved as interpretation layers or future modules in the current version, and no hard judgment will be made. Technical Note's evidence levels are by default divided into: launched product rules, operational indicators being collected, planned stability indicators, and an explanation framework that is only a theoretical background; these levels cannot be mixed into the same certainty.
entries.title: method boundaries

entries.body: Public instructions only use aggregated method metrics and do not expose individual answer payloads, private observation text, or feedback records that can identify individual users. The share page does not display observation private content by default, and user_confirmed_type will not be regarded as the final type of the system. User feedback, sample content, and Technical Note indicators should all comply with the principles of minimum necessity, aggregate display, and traceability; if an indicator is still in the planned or collecting state, the page will only explain the definition and collection direction, and will not display forged numbers.
entries.title: Privacy and data

entries.boundary_copy: Adjacent traction is only used as an expressive color cue near the same primary type, and is not equivalent to formal wing determination, nor can it replace the primary type or Top3 interpretation.
entries.interpretation_boundary: The wing hint is only suitable for helping to read "which side of the same primary type may be closer in expression", and is not suitable for diagnosis, ability evaluation, health level judgment, career screening or relationship risk judgment.
entries.user_facing_boundary: If you see traction on the left and right sides of the primary candidate, you can understand it as the possibility of adjacent types of tone, rhythm or focus in the expression; this does not mean that the system has judged you as a certain wing, nor does it mean that you have a certain subtype.

entries.boundary_copy: The arrow direction bit is currently only used as a placeholder for future modules and does not participate in the interpretation of the current results page, nor does the arrow be written as a judgment of pressure, growth or development path.
entries.user_facing_boundary: The current version will not deduce your pressure direction, growth direction or fixed path based on the arrow; if it is displayed in the future, it will only serve as a theoretical background prompt and require verification in real situations.

entries.boundary_copy: The state spectrum bits are only used for self-calibration and are not equivalent to hard judgment on the development stage.
entries.user_facing_boundary: The system will not directly mark you into a fixed state level; currently it only provides three observation frames: stable, daily, and stressed.

entries.boundary_copy: subtype is temporarily disabled to avoid early hard judgment when evidence is insufficient.
entries.user_facing_boundary: The current version does not give instinctual subtype conclusions, nor does it miswrite lifestyle differences as formal subtype determinations.

entries.average_expression: In ordinary situations, notice when this candidate shapes attention and decisions without assuming that it explains every response.
entries.blind_spot_copy: If Type 1 doesn’t emerge as a major clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: Watch to see if you’re less proactive in using standards, closures, and long-term responsibilities to calibrate your actions when rules are vague, quality drops, or responsibility boundaries are unclear. It's not a judgment that you lack a sense of principle.
entries.core_logic: In Enneagram theory, Type 1 describes attention that often moves toward standards, responsibility, order, and improvement. If this candidate fits, notice when you ask, ‘What would be more responsible or sound here?’ Treat that question as an observation cue, not proof of your motives or a fixed personality.

deep_dive.conflict_pattern: In conflict, you may begin with facts, standards, and what needs to change. Add your feelings, the other person’s perspective, and the actual stakes so the discussion does not collapse into a verdict about who is right.
deep_dive.core_desire: In Enneagram theory, Type 1 describes attention that often moves toward standards, responsibility, order, and improvement. If this candidate fits, notice when you ask, ‘What would be more responsible or sound here?’ Treat that question as an observation cue, not proof of your motives or a fixed personality.
deep_dive.core_fear: Possible pressure cues include missed responsibilities, confusing expectations, relaxed standards, overlooked problems, or effort that does not produce a dependable result. These are situations to observe; the report cannot determine what you fear or turn an inferred concern into psychological fact.
deep_dive.defense_pattern: Under pressure, you may check more often, correct details, tighten expectations, or become less flexible in order to restore order. That response can protect quality, but in a low-risk situation it can also narrow your options. This is an observable tendency, not a diagnosis or a confirmed defense mechanism.
deep_dive.growth_principle: For one non-critical task this week, define the minimum acceptable standard, the risks that truly need protection, and the details that may remain unfinished. Review the factual outcome without turning every flaw into a judgment about yourself.
deep_dive.misread_by_others: Your effort to prevent errors may be heard as criticism or fault-finding. That possibility is a communication hypothesis: check what you intended, what the other person heard, and whether the risk was clear.
deep_dive.recovery_action: Start by separating critical risks from non-critical imperfections. Choose one low-stakes detail to leave alone, then compare the actual outcome with what you predicted.
deep_dive.relationship_script: Reliability, remembering details, and repairing problems may be ways you express care. Check whether the other person experiences those actions as support, correction, or both; type theory cannot infer either person’s needs.
deep_dive.self_misread: You may label every correction as responsibility without separating material risk from preference or aesthetics. Ask what the correction actually protects, what evidence supports the risk, and what would happen if the detail remained imperfect.
deep_dive.stress_signal: Early signals may include repeated checking, sharper reactions to small deviations, difficulty recognizing completion, or physical tension.
deep_dive.thirty_day_experiment: For thirty days, log moments when you want to correct something immediately but choose to observe first. Record the risk level, the actual consequence, and feedback from others, then adjust the strength of the standard from evidence.
deep_dive.work_mechanism: At work, your attention may go first to standards, process gaps, ownership, and acceptable quality. This can explain why calibration matters to you, but it does not establish competence, job fit, or performance.

early_warning_signs.body: You review the same item again even though it already meets the agreed standard.
early_warning_signs.title: Checking the same work repeatedly

early_warning_signs.body: A minor issue begins to feel urgent before its actual impact has been checked.
early_warning_signs.title: Escalating small deviations

early_warning_signs.body: After finishing, your attention stays on the remaining gaps rather than what already meets the requirement.
early_warning_signs.title: Difficulty noticing completion

early_warning_signs.body: Your shoulders, jaw, breathing, or posture may tighten. Treat this as a cue to pause, not a health judgment.
early_warning_signs.title: Physical tension increases

growth_costs.body: Even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect.
growth_costs.title: Treating rest as failure

growth_costs.body: Under pressure, it may be easier to argue from right and wrong than to say you are tired. Include capacity and recovery in the review.
growth_costs.title: Turning fatigue into a principle dispute

growth_costs.body: A no-regrets standard applied everywhere can crowd out experimentation and rest. Reserve the highest bar for work that truly requires it.
growth_costs.title: Letting high standards consume recovery

growth_costs.body: If the first message is what needs fixing, others may miss the care behind it. State the shared aim before the correction.
growth_costs.title: Letting correction hide care

growth_strengths.body: When you explain what a standard protects—quality, fairness, or safety—others can understand your persistence as stewardship rather than fault-finding.
growth_strengths.title: Make standards easier to trust

growth_strengths.body: Your caution can be valuable when safety, commitments, or long-term trust are at stake. In lower-risk situations, distinguish necessary standards from extra effort.
growth_strengths.title: Protect quality at critical points

growth_strengths.body: With enough authority and resources, you may translate problems into clearer processes, documentation, or review practices rather than stopping at criticism.
growth_strengths.title: Turn critique into improvement

growth_strengths.body: Standards can strengthen collaboration when they protect shared boundaries instead of pressuring people or proving who is right.
growth_strengths.title: Use fairness to stabilize cooperation

recovery_protocol.body: Sort issues by consequence, then address only the deviation that most affects the outcome.
recovery_protocol.title: Separate critical from non-critical

recovery_protocol.body: Choose one low-consequence item, stop at the agreed standard, and record what actually happens.
recovery_protocol.title: Practice a low-risk ‘good enough’

recovery_protocol.body: Pause typing, stand up, or move briefly before deciding whether another change is necessary.
recovery_protocol.title: Step out of correction mode

small_experiments.body: Log the other issues without fixing them immediately, then see which ones still matter the next day.
small_experiments.title: Address one critical issue per day

small_experiments.body: Try, ‘Could we look at the risk together?’ before offering your preferred fix.
small_experiments.title: Turn correction into an invitation

small_experiments.body: Each day, note one piece of work that met its purpose without further refinement.
small_experiments.title: Record evidence of sufficiency

The same attention pattern can become costly when even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect.

communication_manual.body: Before pointing out the problem, let’s first talk about what this standard is protecting: less rework, fair division of labor, or preventing risks from being passed through. This makes it easier for the other person to hear your concerns instead of just your corrections.
communication_manual.title: First give the purpose behind the standard

communication_manual.body: If you have three things you want to say, first mark which one must be dealt with and which two are just reminders. Communication will be more like a consultation than a one-time review.
communication_manual.title: Separate musts from recommendations

communication_manual.body: When your tone becomes tougher, you can add, "I'm a little anxious because I'm worried that something will go wrong later." This is not to weaken your position, but to let the other person see that you are not just finding fault.
communication_manual.title: Add your feelings

conflict_trigger_points.body: When the agreed time, division of labor or standards are not fulfilled twice in a row, you may first enter into correction. Check the facts, impact and original agreement first to avoid directly escalating a mistake into a character judgment.
conflict_trigger_points.title: Promises repeatedly broken

conflict_trigger_points.body: You may harden faster when boundaries, processes, or acceptance criteria are temporarily changed. Before conflict, ask: Is this an exception, a trial, or will this be the case in the future?
conflict_trigger_points.title: Temporary changes to rules

conflict_trigger_points.body: When the other person says "it's okay" and "almost" but you see the subsequent risks, it's easy to increase the intensity. First explain the risk level, and then distinguish between the parts that must be repaired and those that can be observed.
conflict_trigger_points.title: Issues downplayed

partner_facing_notes.body: When he repeatedly confirms rules, time, or commitments, he may be putting the relationship into a dependable structure; or it may simply be that the current matter is high-risk. Ask him which step he is most worried about first, rather than directly interpreting it as being picky.
partner_facing_notes.title: Put correction back into specific scenarios

partner_facing_notes.body: If he doesn't remind or correct this time, it doesn't mean he doesn't care; he may also choose to retain flexibility first. You can ask specifically: Do you want me to listen to you now, or do you want me to fix this problem together?
partner_facing_notes.title: If you don’t correct it, you may be leaving space.

relationship_strengths.body: In a relationship with clear agreements and clear responsibilities, it may be easier for you to show that you care by being punctual, honoring your obligations, and handling problems cleanly.
relationship_strengths.title: Put reliability into action

relationship_strengths.body: When an issue will affect each other repeatedly, you may be more willing to discuss it instead of just being superficial. Whether it is helpful still depends on the timing of expression, tone and the state of the other person.
relationship_strengths.title: Willing to face conflicts seriously

relationship_strengths.body: You may quickly see which commitments, proportions or responsibilities need to be clearly stated; this can sometimes reduce misunderstandings, and may also require more explanation of feelings.
relationship_strengths.title: Boundary language is clearer

relationship_strengths.body: Arrangements, reminders, and repairs may be one of the ways you express your care; if the other person needs more emotional response, you still have to go back to the specific interaction to check.
relationship_strengths.title: Attention lies in details

relationship_traps.body: You may be protecting quality or fairness, but if it's an issue right from the start, the other person may feel negated at first. First ask the other person if they are willing to listen to feedback, and then explain the impact of your concerns; repair in the relationship also requires the other person to be willing to respond, rather than just relying on you to make the standards clearer.
relationship_traps.title: Concern is heard as criticism

relationship_traps.body: When you are hurt, you may talk about right and wrong, rules or responsibilities first, but the real disappointment will appear later. You can separate principles and feelings and say: "I feel this is inappropriate and makes me a little disappointed."
relationship_traps.title: Principles cover injuries

relationship_traps.body: When you're anxious to make a relationship better, suggestions may come across as makeover projects. First confirm whether this is something that both parties want to adjust, and avoid taking your ideal order as the only answer to the relationship.
relationship_traps.title: Correction becomes transformation

relationship_traps.body: If you keep suppressing your dissatisfaction in the front, you may increase the intensity all at once later. A more stable approach is to give a light reminder when small deviations occur and give the other person room to explain limitations or misunderstandings.
relationship_traps.title: Hardens after long-term patience

repair_language.body: I just seemed to be finding fault. In fact, what I was worried about was how this incident would affect the next steps. Let me explain the impact clearly first.
repair_language.title: Let me talk about the impact first

repair_language.body: Not every detail needs to be changed right away. Let us first distinguish three categories: must be repaired, can be looked at later, and can be accepted.
repair_language.title: We prioritize

repair_language.body: After I finished talking about the standards, I also want to hear about your restrictions and see how to adjust them in the most practical way this time.
repair_language.title: I also listen to your restrictions

entries.relationship_summary: Reliability, remembering details, and repairing problems may be ways you express care. Check whether the other person experiences those actions as support, correction, or both; type theory cannot infer either person’s needs. In conflict, you may begin with facts, standards, and what needs to change. Add your feelings, the other person’s perspective, and the actual stakes so the discussion does not collapse into a verdict about who is right.
entries.seven_day_question: Over the next 7 days, record a time when you wanted to correct something: were you more worried about quality, responsibility, relationships, or a sense of loss of control?
entries.short_title: Calibrates reality through standards and responsibility
entries.strained_expression: Under heavier load, even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect. This is an observation cue, not a level assignment or diagnosis.
entries.surface_impression: Your effort to prevent errors may be heard as criticism or fault-finding. That possibility is a communication hypothesis: check what you intended, what the other person heard, and whether the risk was clear.
entries.validation_hook: Across the next week, notice the situations described here and record both confirming examples and clear exceptions. A candidate is useful only if it improves observation without flattening context.

collaboration_manual.body: By explaining the risks, impacts, and shared goals before asking a question, you reduce the chance that others will interpret your warning as critical.
collaboration_manual.title: First align “Why should we repair?”

collaboration_manual.body: Dividing suggestions into three categories: need to be addressed, observable, and deferred can help prevent all issues from being pushed to the highest intensity.
collaboration_manual.title: Mark the risk level

collaboration_manual.body: In addition to pointing out deviations, it also explains what state is good enough to make the working boundary clearer.
collaboration_manual.title: Give an acceptable version

ideal_environment.body: The clearer your completion standards, risk levels, and rework conditions are, the more you can focus on high-value issues.
ideal_environment.title: Standards can be discussed

ideal_environment.body: When the team discusses issues with evidence rather than turning feedback into emotional evaluations, your sense of standards is more likely to be caught.
ideal_environment.title: Review based on facts

ideal_environment.body: If the environment allows for 80% delivery and iteration, it is easier for you to practice allocating standard intensity by risk.
ideal_environment.title: Allows distinction between critical and non-critical

leadership_pattern.body: When you are in a leading, coordinating or reminding position, your influence may come from clarifying goals, standards, responsibilities and review mechanisms, so that delivery does not rely solely on personal awareness. It is suitable for use in scenarios where quality risks are high and processes are prone to drift; however, this only affects style cues and does not mean that the system determines that you have leadership capabilities or are suitable for management positions.
leadership_pattern.title: Use standards and review to create influence

leadership_pattern.body: If the feedback only consists of pointing out shortcomings, the team may interpret your advancement as fault-finding. A more stable approach is to explain the risks, trade-offs and next-step criteria at the same time, so that correction becomes a joint learning rather than an individual judgment; whether it is effective also depends on team trust, authorization boundaries and specific expression methods.
leadership_pattern.title: Turn correction into common calibration

managed_by_others.body: When others need to collaborate with you, assign tasks, or make requests, it may be easier to keep you engaged by clearly stating boundaries, priorities, acceptance criteria, and where trial and error are allowed. What is described here is a preference for collaboration. It is not a general prescription for management methods, nor does it necessarily mean that you need a high-control environment.
managed_by_others.title: First align authorization, priority and acceptance criteria

managed_by_others.body: If the standards continue to change, but the accountability remains retroactive, you may get tighter or defensive more quickly. A more negotiable approach is to clearly state the reasons for the change, scope of impact, and adjustment of responsibilities simultaneously, so that corrections can be returned to the facts of the task rather than turning into mutual accusations.
managed_by_others.title: Synchronize responsibilities and basis when changing standards

work_friction_points.body: When you are quick to point out omissions, discrepancies, or inconsistencies, collaborators may first hear "being corrected" rather than hearing that you are protecting the quality of your delivery. A more negotiable approach is to first explain the risks, acceptance criteria, or common goals associated with this piece of feedback, and then distinguish between the parts that must be corrected and those that can be observed later; this is just a clue to communication friction, and it does not mean that you are necessarily picky or that others are necessarily resistant to feedback.
work_friction_points.title: The common goal needs to be stated before reminding

work_friction_points.body: If low-risk details are handled with the same intensity, the team may feel that progress is being slowed down, and you may become drawn further into the details. Problems can be divided into categories such as release risks, rework risks, experience preferences and personal aesthetics, so that standards can become a decision-making tool instead of being equally tight in every scenario.
work_friction_points.title: Standard strength needs to be stratified by risk

work_friction_points.body: When you are not confident about the quality of the delivery, you may repeat inspections, finish the work yourself, or fill in the omissions for others. This can reduce risks in the short term, but may blur the boundaries of responsibility in the long term. A more stable way to collaborate is to clearly write down the inspection items, responsible persons, deadlines and acceptable errors to avoid mistakenly turning your sense of responsibility into the team's unspoken default.
work_friction_points.title: Quality inspection responsibilities need to be explicitly assigned

work_friction_points.body: When standards are unclear, people in charge change, or evaluation criteria are vague, it may be harder to tell when enough is enough. Instead of continuing to pursue complete determination, you can ask for a temporary judgment standard: what must be met in this round, what risks should be accepted, and when to review; this can bring the friction from personality attribution back to the task boundary.
work_friction_points.title: Gray area decision-making requires stopping conditions

work_strengths.body: When requirements, acceptance criteria or delivery standards are still vague, it may be easier for you to break them into checklists, process nodes and review questions to help the team reduce rework.
work_strengths.title: Translate standards into executable steps

work_strengths.body: During pre-delivery reviews, pre-launch inspections, or cross-team handovers, you may first notice inconsistencies, omissions, or gaps in responsibilities.
work_strengths.title: See quality risks in advance

work_strengths.body: When key responsibilities are diluted, verbal commitments change repeatedly, or records of decisions are missing, you may prefer to make boundaries clear and make collaboration less accountable afterwards; whether it is accepted by the team also depends on the way of expression and organizational culture.
work_strengths.title: Maintain boundaries of responsibility

work_strengths.body: During review meetings, quality reviews, or process revisions, you may be used to turning problems into corrective actions instead of just complaining; this is more likely to work in a team that allows for concrete improvements.
work_strengths.title: Drive continuous improvement

workplace_trigger_points.body: When the acceptance criteria, priority, or responsibility boundaries of the same task change repeatedly, and the reasons for the changes are not explained simultaneously, it may be more difficult for you to focus steadily on the delivery itself. This refers to alert cues in the work situation and does not mean that you lack the ability to adapt to change.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Environment: Standards drift frequently

workplace_trigger_points.body: If obvious vulnerabilities, compliance risks, or review conclusions have been ignored for a long time, you may want to increase the intensity of the alerts. The task environment that is more suitable for you usually requires separate discussions between "do it quickly" and "protect the bottom line".
workplace_trigger_points.title: Task: Quality risks are quickly eliminated

workplace_trigger_points.body: When you raise a standard or issue, it may be harder for you to continue to be gentle if the other person directly hears it as critical. At this time, it is necessary to separate the facts, impacts and next step criteria, rather than turning the interaction into who is right and who is wrong.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Relationships: Correction is understood to be personal

entries.work_summary: At work, your attention may go first to standards, process gaps, ownership, and acceptable quality. This can explain why calibration matters to you, but it does not establish competence, job fit, or performance. Observe how the pattern changes with authority, workload, role clarity, and psychological safety.

entries.average_expression: In ordinary situations, notice when this candidate shapes attention and decisions without assuming that it explains every response.
entries.blind_spot_copy: If Type 2 does not become the main clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: observe whether you are less proactive in using support, care, and requests for clarity to maintain connection when others need responses, collaboration needs filling, or the sense of connection cools. It’s not a judgment that you’re aloof or don’t care about the relationship.
entries.core_logic: In Enneagram theory, Type 2 describes attention that often moves toward connection, responsiveness, support, and whether others need care. If this candidate fits, notice when ‘Can I help, and are we still connected?’ becomes your organizing question. It is a clue to observe, not proof of your motives or worth.

deep_dive.conflict_pattern: In conflict, you may focus first on whether the bond has been damaged or whether your effort was seen. State the specific need or disappointment instead of waiting for the other person to infer it.
deep_dive.core_desire: In Enneagram theory, Type 2 describes attention that often moves toward connection, responsiveness, support, and whether others need care. If this candidate fits, notice when ‘Can I help, and are we still connected?’ becomes your organizing question. It is a clue to observe, not proof of your motives or worth.
deep_dive.core_fear: Possible pressure cues include an unacknowledged contribution, a delayed response, a cooler relationship, or uncertainty about whether your help is wanted. The report cannot determine what you fear or reduce your relational life to one motive.
deep_dive.defense_pattern: Under pressure, you may offer more help, move closer, anticipate needs, or place your own needs later in order to restore connection. That can support cooperation, but it can also make limits and requests harder to see. This is an observation hypothesis, not a diagnosis.
deep_dive.growth_principle: Before helping this week, check what support is actually wanted, what capacity you have, and what response you hope for. If the response is unclear, ask rather than adding more effort automatically.
deep_dive.misread_by_others: Generous support may be taken for granted, while disappointment is dismissed as overreaction. Treat that as a possible interaction gap and check what was offered, what was expected, and what was actually communicated.
deep_dive.recovery_action: Begin with one clear boundary or request: say what you can offer, what you cannot take on, and what response would help.
deep_dive.relationship_script: Checking in, remembering details, and offering practical support may be ways you express care. Keep your capacity and your own needs visible so care remains a choice rather than an unspoken contract.
deep_dive.self_misread: You may call every act of helping freely chosen even when obligation, fear of distance, or a wish for recognition is also present. Ask what you genuinely want to offer and what request you have not yet made.
deep_dive.stress_signal: Early signals may include agreeing too quickly, difficulty declining requests, tracking whether effort is noticed, or hoping others will identify a need you have not named.
deep_dive.thirty_day_experiment: For thirty days, record one moment each day when you paused before helping. Note whether you chose to help, set a limit, or make a request, and what happened to the relationship afterward.
deep_dive.work_mechanism: At work, you may notice unmet support needs, handoff gaps, and shifts in team dynamics early. This attention pattern does not establish job fit, competence, or performance.

early_warning_signs.body: You say yes before considering time, energy, and responsibility boundaries.
early_warning_signs.title: Agreeing before checking capacity

early_warning_signs.body: Your attention shifts toward how much you have done and whether it was noticed instead of checking expectations directly.
early_warning_signs.title: Keeping score internally

early_warning_signs.body: You wait for someone to notice what you need rather than making a specific request.
early_warning_signs.title: Hoping others will infer your need

early_warning_signs.body: You keep responding or helping even when you are already depleted.
early_warning_signs.title: Continuing after your energy is gone

growth_costs.body: When connection feels uncertain, doing more can become a way to prove importance. Separate the value of your support from your value as a person.
growth_costs.title: Using effort to secure a place

growth_costs.body: If a need remains unspoken, others may not know how to respond. Translate the need into a specific, answerable request.
growth_costs.title: Waiting to be noticed

growth_costs.body: A limit may feel like a relational failure even when your capacity is genuinely low. Distinguish available energy from care and commitment.
growth_costs.title: Feeling guilty about limits

growth_costs.body: When effort goes unacknowledged, irritation can accumulate. Name the expectation before it turns into a silent account of who owes what.
growth_costs.title: Letting disappointment become resentment

growth_strengths.body: In familiar or high-contact settings, you may pick up on unspoken difficulty. Confirm by asking instead of deciding for the other person.
growth_strengths.title: Notice needs early

growth_strengths.body: When help is wanted and you have capacity, you may turn care into useful action, resources, or steady presence.
growth_strengths.title: Make support concrete

growth_strengths.body: When tension is still workable, you may help reopen contact before misunderstanding grows.
growth_strengths.title: Repair connection

growth_strengths.body: When pace or output dominates, you may remind a team to consider human impact without taking responsibility for everyone’s emotions.
growth_strengths.title: Keep people visible in the work

recovery_protocol.body: Before responding, distinguish willingness, genuine responsibility, and fear that the relationship will change.
recovery_protocol.title: Ask whether the help is freely chosen

recovery_protocol.body: State what you want in concrete terms instead of asking the other person to guess.
recovery_protocol.title: Make one answerable request

recovery_protocol.body: Reserve time that is not available for supporting others, and communicate that boundary clearly.
recovery_protocol.title: Protect recovery time

small_experiments.body: Give yourself a short pause to decide whether you can realistically take the request on.
small_experiments.title: Wait ten minutes before agreeing

small_experiments.body: Say, ‘I can’t do that this time,’ and observe what actually happens to the relationship.
small_experiments.title: Practice one low-stakes no

small_experiments.body: Invite the other person to say what helped and what did not, so usefulness is not measured only through gratitude.
small_experiments.title: Ask for specific feedback

communication_manual.body: Don't let the other person guess what they need from your efforts. Directly saying "What do I want you to respond to this time?" is easier to catch than continuing to provide additional care.
communication_manual.title: Turn expectations into requests

communication_manual.body: When you offer to help, also make it clear where you can go and when you need to stop. The clearer the boundaries, the less likely support will turn into an afterthought.
communication_manual.title: First explain the support boundaries

communication_manual.body: You can say "I took the initiative to coordinate these two times, but I didn't get a response, so I was a little disappointed." Concrete facts can reduce the feeling of accusation and let the other person know where to respond.
communication_manual.title: Put the loss next to the facts

conflict_trigger_points.body: After you continuously fill in the gaps, coordinate or take care of details, if the other person does not respond, frustration will easily accumulate. Point out the specific incident first rather than waiting for the emotion to turn into a bill.
conflict_trigger_points.title: The dedication is not seen

conflict_trigger_points.body: When you ask for support and are rejected, you may interpret the rejection as meaning that you are not important. First confirm which thing, time, or relationship the other person is rejecting.
conflict_trigger_points.title: Request denied

conflict_trigger_points.body: When your messages get shorter, your meetings less frequent, or your tone softens, you may want to double down on your efforts. Ask about the reasons for the changes before deciding whether you need more support.
conflict_trigger_points.title: Response suddenly decreased

partner_facing_notes.body: When he takes the initiative to fill in, asks how he feels, or remembers details, he may be expressing his approach; or it may be that this time the responsibility really falls on him. When responding, state clearly what you saw and ask him what he can do.
partner_facing_notes.title: Treat support as a negotiable behavior

partner_facing_notes.body: If he refuses, withholds care, or doesn't respond right away, it doesn't automatically mean he doesn't care. A more reliable way to check is to ask: Do you need space, help, or a specific response from me this time?
partner_facing_notes.title: Distance does not necessarily equal a cooling relationship

relationship_strengths.body: When the other person needs support or the interaction becomes cold, you may be more likely to take the initiative to approach, ask, and fill in; this shows a tendency to pay attention, but it does not mean that you must be responsible for maintaining the temperature of the relationship.
relationship_strengths.title: Proactively respond to relationship signals

relationship_strengths.body: You may notice more quickly when responses decrease, tone changes, or distance increases; these clues need to be confirmed by questioning and cannot be directly taken as the other person’s true thoughts.
relationship_strengths.title: Detect interaction changes earlier

relationship_strengths.body: You might express proximity by remembering preferences, arranging small things, or tending to practical needs; this advantage is more stable when reciprocity and boundaries are clear.
relationship_strengths.title: Express care with details

relationship_strengths.body: When there are cracks in the relationship, you may be willing to open the door to communication first; whether the repair is effective still depends on whether both parties are willing to participate, not on you alone to do more.
relationship_strengths.title: Willing to try to repair the connection

relationship_traps.body: You may express closeness with care, but unspoken needs are difficult to respond to accurately. Replace "I've done so much" in advance with "I need you to help me with something this time."
relationship_traps.title: Need to hide and pay

relationship_traps.body: It is natural to want to be actively seen, but if understanding is taken as proof of love or not, the relationship will become difficult to calibrate. Check first to see if the other person knows what you expect, and then judge whether the response is adequate.
relationship_traps.title: Expect the other person to take the initiative to understand

relationship_traps.body: In order to stay connected, you may take on care that exceeds your physical strength, time, or inclination. Clarify the scope before supporting. Reciprocity does not mean reciprocity every time, but it cannot be borne by only one party for a long time.
relationship_traps.title: Boundaries are diluted by intimacy

relationship_traps.body: After suppressing needs for a long time, expressing can easily turn into rehashing old scores. You can start with a recent specific incident and explain how you hope to share the burden in the future, rather than just proving that you have paid a lot.
relationship_traps.title: Grief with a sense of bill

repair_language.body: I didn't make it clear just now. I actually hope you can respond to this specific matter, rather than asking you to guess what I need.
repair_language.title: I express my expectations

repair_language.body: I am willing to help with these few things, but I need to stop for the rest, or we can arrange for someone else to take over.
repair_language.title: Re-clarification of support scope

repair_language.body: I'm a little disappointed, but I don't want to do more in exchange for a response. Let’s just tell each other what we need this time.
repair_language.title: I won’t pay more for now

entries.relationship_summary: Checking in, remembering details, and offering practical support may be ways you express care. Keep your capacity and your own needs visible so care remains a choice rather than an unspoken contract. In conflict, you may focus first on whether the bond has been damaged or whether your effort was seen. State the specific need or disappointment instead of waiting for the other person to infer it.
entries.seven_day_question: Over the next seven days, record a time when you wanted to do a little more: was that out of a genuine desire, fear of losing connection, or not knowing how to ask directly?
entries.short_title: Tracks connection through response and support
entries.strained_expression: Under heavier load, when connection feels uncertain, doing more can become a way to prove importance. Separate the value of your support from your value as a person. This is an observation cue, not a level assignment or diagnosis.
entries.surface_impression: Generous support may be taken for granted, while disappointment is dismissed as overreaction. Treat that as a possible interaction gap and check what was offered, what was expected, and what was actually communicated.
entries.validation_hook: Across the next week, notice the situations described here and record both confirming examples and clear exceptions. A candidate is useful only if it improves observation without flattening context.

collaboration_manual.body: Confirming what the other person actually needs before supporting can reduce the burden of taking too much responsibility for others.
collaboration_manual.title: Ask first if you are needed

collaboration_manual.body: If you want the other person to respond or cooperate, it's clearer to say it directly than to wait for a long time.
collaboration_manual.title: Speak out your expectations

collaboration_manual.body: Being clear about what you can and cannot do protects relationships and energy.
collaboration_manual.title: Set support boundaries

ideal_environment.body: If the team can clearly recognize coordination, user care, and relationship maintenance, it will be easier for you to stay committed.
ideal_environment.title: Support labor to be seen

ideal_environment.body: When rejections, scheduling, and resource constraints can be discussed normally, you don't have to overpay to maintain the relationship.
ideal_environment.title: Boundaries can be respected

ideal_environment.body: A clear response can help you determine whether your input is effective more than a generic thank you.
ideal_environment.title: Feedback is specific and timely

leadership_pattern.body: When you are in a leading or coordinating position, influence can come from seeing member status, connecting resources, tending to a collaborative atmosphere, and making asking for help more likely to occur. It can help teams feel less isolated, but it cannot be understood as a natural fit for managing others, nor is it a substitute for goals, authority, and evidence of performance.
leadership_pattern.title: Use support networks to create influence

leadership_pattern.body: If you are used to using fill-in, comfort, or additional support to maintain progress, the team may be smoother in the short term, but in the long term it will be unclear who is really responsible. A more sustainable way to influence is to explain the scope of support, handover conditions and responsibility boundaries so that investment in the relationship does not become a unspoken default.
leadership_pattern.title: Separate care and empowerment

managed_by_others.body: When others give feedback on your input, pointing out what specific support you have provided and what problems you have solved is usually more likely to be accepted than simply saying "Thank you for your hard work." It indicates your preference for feedback, and it does not mean that you can only rely on external recognition to maintain motivation.
managed_by_others.title: Reduce recognition to specific supporting behaviors

managed_by_others.body: If all coordination, reassurance, or temporary care falls to you by default, you may become increasingly exhausted and find it harder to say no. During collaboration, the time, scope and subsequent successors of the replacement can be clarified to avoid turning relationship investment into invisible responsibilities.
managed_by_others.title: Temporary filling requires confirmation of boundaries

work_friction_points.body: When the team assumes that you will coordinate, comfort, fill in, or take care of emotions, invisible labor will easily accumulate. You can make it clear "what I can support, what I cannot take over in the long term, and who needs to take over", so that help can be returned to assignable tasks instead of becoming a default request for investment in your relationship.
work_friction_points.title: Support work needs to be seen and assigned

work_friction_points.body: If there is no response for a long time, it may be more difficult for you to judge whether you have helped the key points, or you may interpret silence as not being needed. A more practical approach is to agree on a feedback method, such as "Did the support solve the problem this time? Do I need to intervene next time?" to avoid relying solely on a sense of recognition to judge the value of cooperation.
work_friction_points.title: Feedback channels need to be specified

work_friction_points.body: When someone else makes a request, you may see the other person's needs first and evaluate your own capacity later. Rejection can be changed into boundary negotiation: explaining the scope of what can be provided, what cannot be undertaken, and alternative paths; this not only retains the sense of connection, but also reduces the subsequent friction caused by over-commitment.
work_friction_points.title: Rejection can be changed to boundary negotiation

work_friction_points.body: In order to prevent the relationship from becoming tense, you may delay expressing your disagreement until the problem becomes larger before expressing it all at once. During collaboration, you can express reservations in a low-intensity way in advance, such as "I support this direction, but there is a boundary that needs to be made clear first."
work_friction_points.title: Dissent needs to arise in advance

work_strengths.body: When new people take over, cross-department collaboration occurs, or there is a gap in information transmission, you may be more likely to notice who is stuck, who lacks information, and where support is needed.
work_strengths.title: Seeing gaps in collaboration

work_strengths.body: During rush hours, post-conflict or long-term project exhaustion periods, you may take the initiative to add care, confirm feelings and coordinate communication so that cooperation is not just about delivery; you also need to be careful not to take all the maintenance of relationships on yourself.
work_strengths.title: Maintain team temperature

work_strengths.body: In client conversations, team rituals, or one-on-one collaborations, you may be more likely to remember preferences, concerns, and unspoken needs; these clues help inform communication but do not equate to career fit conclusions.
work_strengths.title: Remember people's details

work_strengths.body: When colleagues encounter obstacles, you often not only say "I understand", but also turn it into concrete help, reminders, resource connections or follow-up; when boundaries are clear, this kind of support is less likely to turn into over-burdening.
work_strengths.title: Put support into action

workplace_trigger_points.body: When the team leaves coordination, emotional care, and temporary closing to you by default without confirming time and boundaries, you may gradually be consumed. What is described here is the role load, not that you have to take on the support role.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Environment: Invisible filling becomes the default

workplace_trigger_points.body: If you invest heavily in communicating, connecting resources, or helping others move forward, but these efforts are never factored into planning and feedback, it may be harder to judge how much to continue investing.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Task: Support work is not included in the priority list

workplace_trigger_points.body: When the other person changes from intensive interaction to cold treatment, or only accepts help without explaining the true needs, you may want to take the initiative to get closer to confirm. A safer approach is to ask for specific feedback rather than automatically increasing efforts.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Relationships: Responses suddenly become cold or vague

entries.work_summary: At work, you may notice unmet support needs, handoff gaps, and shifts in team dynamics early. This attention pattern does not establish job fit, competence, or performance. Observe how the pattern changes with authority, workload, role clarity, and psychological safety.

entries.average_expression: In ordinary situations, notice when this candidate shapes attention and decisions without assuming that it explains every response.
entries.blind_spot_copy: If Type 3 does not emerge as a major clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: observe whether you are less proactive in using progress, results, and external evaluation to calibrate actions when goals need to be aligned, results need to be presented, or feedback affects the next step. It is not a judgment that you are unmotivated or incompetent.
entries.core_logic: In Enneagram theory, Type 3 describes attention that often moves toward goals, results, feedback, and visible effectiveness. If this candidate fits, notice when ‘What will move this forward, and how will success be recognized?’ organizes your choices. It is an observation cue, not a verdict on your worth.

deep_dive.conflict_pattern: In conflict, you may move first toward resolution and restored performance. Slow down enough to name the emotional impact and let the other person shape the next step.
deep_dive.core_desire: In Enneagram theory, Type 3 describes attention that often moves toward goals, results, feedback, and visible effectiveness. If this candidate fits, notice when ‘What will move this forward, and how will success be recognized?’ organizes your choices. It is an observation cue, not a verdict on your worth.
deep_dive.core_fear: Possible pressure cues include failure, absent feedback, invisible work, stalled progress, or a gap between how you feel and how you appear. The report cannot determine what you fear or tie your value to achievement.
deep_dive.defense_pattern: Under pressure, you may accelerate, sharpen your presentation, emphasize results, suppress fatigue, or move quickly to the next goal. That can produce momentum, but it can also postpone feelings and relationship needs. This is an observable tendency, not a diagnosis.
deep_dive.growth_principle: Before accelerating this week, name the value the result is meant to serve and one cost you are unwilling to hide. Build recovery and candid feedback into the plan.
deep_dive.misread_by_others: Others may see only efficiency or performance and miss the pressure you are carrying. Treat that as a communication hypothesis and check what you showed, what you withheld, and what support was available.
deep_dive.recovery_action: Take a pause with no presenting, optimizing, or proving. Name what you need, what resources remain, and which value the next action should serve.
deep_dive.relationship_script: Taking responsibility, solving practical problems, and creating better conditions may be ways you express care. Check whether emotional presence and mutual influence remain part of the relationship.
deep_dive.self_misread: You may treat visible progress as the only reliable measure of value. Ask whether the goal still serves something important and whether the pace is sustainable.
deep_dive.stress_signal: Early signals may include constant optimization, repeated checking for feedback, hiding obstacles, or feeling guilty when you stop.
deep_dive.thirty_day_experiment: For thirty days, record one choice made for long-term value rather than visibility. Note the result, the emotional cost, and whether your relationships or recovery changed.
deep_dive.work_mechanism: At work, your attention may move quickly to goals, feedback, resources, and the path to delivery. This preference does not establish competence, job fit, or performance.

early_warning_signs.body: As soon as one task is done, you optimize it further or replace it with another goal.
early_warning_signs.title: Moving immediately to the next target

early_warning_signs.body: When feedback is quiet, you repeatedly check the result, add explanations, or gather more proof.
early_warning_signs.title: Seeking repeated confirmation

early_warning_signs.body: You preserve the appearance of normal progress instead of naming where you are stuck or asking for help.
early_warning_signs.title: Keeping obstacles out of view

early_warning_signs.body: Rest quickly feels like falling behind, wasting time, or showing insufficient commitment.
early_warning_signs.title: Feeling guilty about recovery

growth_costs.body: A disappointing result may begin to feel like evidence about your worth. Review the goal, resources, and external conditions separately.
growth_costs.title: Tying value to outcomes

growth_costs.body: A fast work rhythm can delay awareness of fatigue, disappointment, or reluctance. Add a state check beside the progress check.
growth_costs.title: Discovering feelings late

growth_costs.body: If you hide uncertainty or obstacles, support arrives later and the real risk stays invisible.
growth_costs.title: Spending energy on appearing capable

growth_costs.body: Someone close to you may need to be heard before a solution is built. Efficiency is not the same as relational responsiveness.
growth_costs.title: Turning relationships into tasks

growth_strengths.body: When goals and feedback are clear, you may translate plans into visible progress quickly.
growth_strengths.title: Turn goals into delivery

growth_strengths.body: You may adjust strategy rapidly when the criteria are credible. When feedback is ambiguous, clarify the standard before adapting.
growth_strengths.title: Adapt to useful feedback

growth_strengths.body: A clear sense of purpose can help a team see the next step without requiring everyone to match the same pace.
growth_strengths.title: Create forward momentum

growth_strengths.body: When resources are limited, you may identify the highest-leverage work while still accounting for process and relationship costs.
growth_strengths.title: Focus resources on impact

recovery_protocol.body: Set a defined period with no presenting, optimizing, or reporting, and decide in advance when you will return.
recovery_protocol.title: Pause performance work

recovery_protocol.body: Write down whether you need recognition, rest, support, or a different definition of success.
recovery_protocol.title: Name the need beneath the goal

recovery_protocol.body: Ask whether the work still serves a long-term value and fits current resources, independent of comparison.
recovery_protocol.title: Review value rather than rank

small_experiments.body: After completing it, wait ten minutes before making any cosmetic improvement and observe the urge to continue.
small_experiments.title: Leave one finished item unpolished

small_experiments.body: Name an unresolved problem to a trusted person and observe whether honesty actually reduces your value in their eyes.
small_experiments.title: Disclose one obstacle

small_experiments.body: Record one period each day whose value is recovery, reflection, or connection rather than output.
small_experiments.title: Protect non-productive time

state_spectrum_copy.stable_expression: With more capacity and choice, when goals and feedback are clear, you may translate plans into visible progress quickly.
state_spectrum_copy.strained_expression: Under heavier load, a disappointing result may begin to feel like evidence about your worth. Review the goal, resources, and external conditions separately. This is an observation cue, not a level assignment or diagnosis.
